summary: Describes three ways for a TURN client to discover TURN servers automatically, instead of relying on explicit configuration. This lets enterprises and ISPs offer their own servers. It updates RFC 5766 to relax the mutual authentication requirement in certain cases.

eli5.summary: When your phone needs a helper to pass messages through a firewall, it used to need the helper's address typed in. Now it can find one on its own.

questions: how to auto discover a turn server
how does a turn client discover servers
what is the turn anycast address
how does dns sd find a turn server
subtitle: Three ways for a TURN client to find a relay server on its own, plus a relaxed authentication rule for network-provided servers.

tldr.problem: TURN clients are usually configured with a well-known TURN server, so enterprises and ISPs that want to offer their own servers have no way for clients to discover them with little or no configuration.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three discovery mechanisms: S-NAPTR service resolution using a domain name learned from DHCP or the user's identity, DNS Service Discovery including mDNS, and a well-known anycast address that redirects the client to a unicast server.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 5766 so STUN authentication becomes optional for network-provided TURN servers, which opens them to attacks unless operators protect them.

today: RFC 8155 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2017 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 5766 by relaxing the mutual authentication requirement for network-provided TURN servers.

sections.title: Why Discover TURN Servers
sections.content:
TURN (RFC 5766) improves the connectivity of peer-to-peer applications by relaying traffic when one or both sides cannot connect directly. It is an important building block for real-time audio, video and collaboration. The RFC notes that no means existed to discover TURN servers automatically, so clients were explicitly configured, usually under the control of the application or TURN service provider rather than the enterprise, ISP or network the client sits in.

This document describes three mechanisms, chosen to maximize the chance of discovery depending on the network: S-NAPTR service resolution, DNS Service Discovery, and an anycast address. WebRTC applications are named as a motivating case.
sections.eli5: Until now, you had to be told the address of the helper who passes messages around the firewall. This RFC lets your phone find one by itself.

sections.title: The Discovery Procedure
sections.content:
By default, a TURN client uses local or manual configuration, which includes servers specified by a web application such as a JavaScript-specified WebRTC server. A client can use auto-discovery when there is no local configuration, when the configuration does not work, or in addition to it. The RFC gives no recommendation on server selection.

The three mechanisms are service resolution (using the host's DNS domain), DNS-SD, and anycast. Not all servers can be found by NAPTR records or DNS-SD, and not all support anycast, so for best results a client SHOULD implement all of them. No strict order is prescribed: a client may run them in parallel, or in any order and stop at the first success. On hosts with more than one interface or address family the procedure runs for each combination.
sections.eli5: You can look for a helper three different ways. You can try them all at once, or one after the other until one works.

sections.title: Discovery Using Service Resolution
sections.content:
This mechanism has two steps: get a DNS domain name for each interface and address family, then do S-NAPTR lookups on it as described in RFC 5928.

For the domain name, the client can use DHCP. RFC 5986 defines the access network domain name options OPTION_V4_ACCESS_DOMAIN and OPTION_V6_ACCESS_DOMAIN. For IPv4 the client MUST request the access network domain name option in a Parameter Request List option, and MAY request the ordinary DHCP domain name option if the access one is not available. For IPv6 it MUST request the option in an Options Request Option within an Information-request message. If neither can be retrieved, the procedure fails for that interface. Alternatively, the client may extract the domain from its own identity, for example example.com from sip:alice@example.com or an email address.

The lookup uses the RELAY application service and the desired protocol tag. If no TURN-specific S-NAPTR records are found, discovery fails for that domain, and the client must wait an appropriate time before retrying a failed lookup.
sections.eli5: First your phone learns the name of the network it is on, like reading the sign on the building. Then it asks the network's phone book where the helper sits.

sections.title: DNS Service Discovery and mDNS
sections.content:
DNS-based Service Discovery (RFC 6763) and Multicast DNS (RFC 6762) give generic ways to find services on a local network. A service instance name has the form <Instance>.<Service>.<Domain>, and for TURN the service part MUST be _turn._udp, _turn._tcp, _turns._udp or _turns._tcp.

With mDNS, a client can multicast a PTR query for these names under local.. A TURN server can also send gratuitous multicast DNS answers when it starts up, wakes from sleep, or detects a change in network configuration, and clients cache what they receive.
sections.eli5: Your phone shouts into the room, "Is there a helper here?" and any helper that hears it shouts back its address.

sections.title: Discovery Using Anycast
sections.content:
A packet sent to an anycast address is delivered to the topologically nearest interface with that address. A client that needs TURN sends a TURN Allocation request to the assigned anycast address. The anycast server performs checks 1 through 7 from Section 6.2 of RFC 5766. If they pass, it MUST reply with a 300 (Try Alternate) error whose ALTERNATE-SERVER attribute holds the server's unicast address, and the client uses that address afterwards. This is needed because two packets sent to an anycast address might reach different servers, so the client also needs to make sure the initial request fits in a single packet.

IANA assigned 192.0.0.10/32 for IPv4 and 2001:1::2/128 for IPv6, both named "Traversal Using Relays around NAT Anycast" and allocated in 2017-02.
sections.eli5: It is like calling one well-known number. Whoever is closest picks up and says, "Call this other number to reach me directly."

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
A change of IP address, for example on a mobile host, may invalidate earlier discovery results, so the client may need to rerun discovery without relying on earlier information. If an earlier learned server is still reachable from the new address, the mobility procedures of RFC 8016 can be used for ongoing streams.

WebRTC endpoints SHOULD treat any TURN server discovered through these mechanisms as an enterprise/gateway or access network server, in line with Recursively Encapsulated TURN.
sections.eli5: If you walk to a new building, the helper you found may not be nearby anymore, so you ask again.

sections.title: Security Considerations and the Update to RFC 5766
sections.content:
STUN authentication is OPTIONAL for TURN servers provided by the local or access network. This downgrades a MUST in RFC 5766, so that new and guest users without long-term credentials can use the service. The RFC admits it opens the server to attacks described in RFC 5766, so such a server must be configured to process requests only from the trusted local network or subscribers, with measures like access lists, firewalls, subscriber quota limits and ingress filtering.

A client without STUN long-term credentials or the third-party authorization extension (RFC 7635) MUST use (D)TLS unless it trusts the network to defend against those attacks, and it is RECOMMENDED to validate the server with trust anchors, SPKI fingerprints or raw public keys. A client MUST NOT fall back to clear text, or to encryption-only, without explicit administrator choice.

An auto-discovered server is only as trusted as the path to it, and MUST NOT be used for privacy-sensitive communication if it falls outside the user's privacy criteria. For anycast, requests may leak onto the Internet if no server knows the address, and a well-known address lets border gateways block them. Sensitive clients can set a limited IP TTL.
sections.eli5: A helper run by the building may let anyone in, even guests with no pass, so the building has to guard it well. Your phone should only trust a helper it can check.

items.title: Service Resolution
items.text: S-NAPTR lookup with the RELAY service, using a domain name from DHCP or the user's identity.

items.title: DNS Service Discovery
items.text: Names such as _turn._udp and _turns._tcp, including multicast queries under local.

items.title: Anycast
items.text: Send an Allocation request to a well-known anycast address and follow the 300 (Try Alternate) reply.
